 CTA Clears Path for Two Rehab Projects, Announces Completion of Third
 Written by Marybeth Luczak, Executive Editor, Railway Age 
 CTA 
 The Chicago Transit Authority is launching the next phase of the Blue Line ’s Forest Park Branch Rebuild Project and the California Station Accessibility and Modernization Project, and reported the wrap up of Lake Street Bridge west leaf reconstruction. 
 The Chicago Transit Board at its Oct. 27 meeting approved a contract award to AECOM Technical Services for the remaining track design work on the Forest Park Branch of the Blue Line from the Illinois Medical District (IMD) station to the I-290 Bridge. This is the next phase of the Forest Park Branch Rebuild Project , which is reconstructing the entire branch, making it 100% accessible to riders using mobility devices. Currently, more than 80% of the branch is categorized as a “slow zone,” according to CTA. 
 (Courtesy of CTA) 
 The first phase of work, which kicked off in 2023, encompassed track and drainage renewals between the UIC-Halsted and IMD stations alongside a modernization and ADA-accessibility rebuild of the Racine station; it featured a $268 million rebuild of three miles of track between the IMD and LaSalle Station downtown.
 Now, AECOM Technical Services will handle design work covering about 70,000 track feet, or about 13 miles between the IMD station and the I-290 Bridge, which is located just east of River Road to the east of the Forest Park station. The contract includes a field investigation of the entire corridor and design for new and upgraded infrastructure, including track, signals, traction power, drainage, utilities, and any other facilities within the CTA right-of-way. It also includes a review of drainage elements along the I-290 expressway shoulders and how they affect CTA rail service.
 AECOM has partnered with three local DBE firms that account for more than 15% of the contract: DB Sterling Consultants, Facet Engineering, and GSG Consultants.
 Funding for the project comes in part from a $15.8 million grant from the Federal Highway Administration’s Carbon Reduction Grant Program, according to CTA. The Illinois Department of Transportation (IDOT) applied on CTA’s behalf and was awarded funding to support the design of future track work on the Blue Line Forest Park Branch. The two agencies authorized an intergovernmental agreement to transfer the funding in July .
 Design work on the two-mile stretch excluded from this contract from Kedzie Avenue to Keeler Avenue has been completed and construction is expected to begin on that segment in 2027, with the support of federal funds from the Reconnecting Communities Program, CTA reported.
 “This track design work is a critical next step in the ongoing partnership with CTA and IDOT to revitalize the I-290 and Forest Park Branch Blue Line corridor,” according to CTA, which is a lead agency with the Chicago Metropolitan Agency for Planning (CMAP) and IDOT on the Connect 290 Blue Program that was established in 2024 to coordinate funding and rebuilding the I-290 Eisenhower Expressway and the Forest Park Branch of the Blue Line. More than 4 million transit riders travel through the corridor annually, and the expressway is said to be one of the most congested in the United States.
 Much of the infrastructure along the Forest Park Branch is original, dating back to 1958, when Dwight D. Eisenhower was President. While CTA said it has performed routine maintenance and made “modest improvements” in recent decades, most of the infrastructure is “far beyond its useful life and needs replacement and upgrades to address issues affecting daily service.”
 “I know how much fast, reliable rail service means for the people and communities we serve,” CTA Acting President Nora Leerhsen said. “This contract is an investment that will build on the improvements we’ve already delivered and moves us closer to our goal of a modernized and accessible Blue Line. We are excited to move forward in our work to strengthen this vital connection between Chicago and the western suburbs.”
 California Blue Line station rendering, courtesy of CTA. 
 Also on Oct. 27, the Chicago Transit Board approved a construction contract to F.H. Paschen, S.N. Nielsen & Associates, LLC for modernization and accessibility improvements at the California Blue Line station, with work set to begin in fourth-quarter 2027. The project is part of CTA’s All Stations Accessibility Program .
 Originally constructed in 1895 and renovated in 2015, the California Blue Line station at 2211 N. California Avenue is said to be one of the busier stations along the line with more than 1.125 million entries in 2025.
 The station upgrade will feature two new elevators serving the inbound and outbound platforms; new stairs and accessible doors; updated signage and wayfinding; platform and canopy extensions, with related adjustments to lighting, railings and windbreaks; and improvements to sidewalks, ramps, drainage and landscaping.
 California Blue Line station renderings, courtesy of CTA. 
 Crews will build a temporary stationhouse and entrance at St. George’s Court for riders to use while work proceeds on the permanent, accessible entrance.
 CTA said the overall value of the contract is not to exceed $39.9 million and will be paid for by a combination of IDOT and City of Chicago Tax Increment Financing (TIF) funds.
 CTA currently operates a 100% accessible bus and rail fleet, and 110 of CTA’s 146 rail stations (75%) are fully accessible, which the agency said is among the highest for legacy transit systems in the United States. The agency’s ASAP Strategic Plan serves as a blueprint for making all rail stations fully accessible by 2038. The California station is among 15 stations that have either recently opened or are currently funded and in various stages of planning, design, or construction under the initiative.
 “An accessible CTA gives more people the freedom to travel independently and connects them to everything our region has to offer,” Nora Leerhsen said. “This investment will bring that promise to life at the California Blue Line station, delivering a modern, welcoming station that better serves riders with disabilities and the entire community.”
 Lake Street Bascule Bridge. (Courtesy of the City of Chicago) 
 Meanwhile, CTA on Oct. 29 reported that the Chicago Department of Transportation (CDOT) has completed installation of the new west leaf of the Lake Street Bascule Bridge , marking a milestone in the ongoing rehabilitation of the 110-year-old bridge.
 June 2026: Off-site construction of the bridge’s west leaf. (Courtesy of the City of Chicago) 
 The new, prefabricated west leaf was assembled off site and transported up the Chicago River by barge. Crews removed the existing leaf, then positioned and installed the replacement during a temporary CTA Green and Pink line shutdown. Work also included aligning and stabilizing the new components; rebuilding CTA tracks, ties, guard systems and walkways; reconnecting and testing power and signal systems; and operating test trains before regular service resumed, according to CTA. 
 Built in 1916, the Lake Street Bridge is a double-deck, double-leaf, movable bridge that accommodates river traffic, and carries vehicles, pedestrians and CTA buses on its lower level and CTA Green and Pink line trains on its upper level. The two-year project will fully rehabilitate the structure. 
 Installation of the bridge’s east leaf is planned for spring 2027. The bridge’s lower level remains closed to vehicles and pedestrians while rehabilitation continues. It is expected to fully reopen in January 2028.
